::: {.lede}
You cannot tickle yourself. Behind that familiar observation there is a
mechanism the laboratory can turn into a number, and where that mechanism
weakens, psychiatric symptoms appear.
:::

Tickling is the most familiar form of it but not the whole of it. I am a
psychiatry resident and I work on this measure through my thesis, so what
follows is both what the literature says and what I learned building the rig
myself. The precision language used here is set out at more length in the [HGF
note](hierarchical-gaussian-filter.qmd); the rig itself is on the [instrument
page](../tools/force-matching.qmd).

## Why your own touch is different {.k-head}

There is no physical difference between touching your own palm and having
someone else touch it the same way. The pressure, the skin and the receptors are
the same. The only thing that changes is where the touch came from, and that is
exactly what lowers the perceived intensity.

Blakemore and colleagues looked at this in 1998. Somatosensory cortex was more
active for externally produced touch and less active for self-produced touch. In
the cerebellum the pattern reversed: cerebellar activity was lower for movements
that produced a touch than for movements that did not. The reading is that
the cerebellum works out the sensory consequence of a movement in advance and
that this is used to turn the incoming signal down. I say reading because the
study does not show that directly; it is only the simplest account that fits
what was found.

The name for that turning down is sensory attenuation. To see what it is for it
helps to remember that most of the signal reaching your senses is produced by
your own movements. If all of it were processed at equal weight, the externally
caused signal, the one that actually carries news, would be lost inside it.
Noise-cancelling headphones do much the same thing, predicting the incoming
sound and generating its inverse, so that only what they could not predict is
left.

## How the task turns it into a number {.k-head}

The most memorable demonstration involved two people. In 2003 Shergill and
colleagues had participants take turns pressing on each other's finger, each
trying to apply the force they had just felt, and the force grew every turn.
Nobody was exaggerating, everyone matched what they felt, but because they felt
their own output as weaker than it was, each put in a little more. The paper's
title sums it up as two eyes for an eye. Which means the line we all used as
children, that he hit first and he hit harder, turns out to have been a
calibration problem rather than a lie.

The same effect was turned into a standard single-person task. In the
force-matching task a target force is applied to the participant's finger and
they are then asked to reproduce it two ways. In the direct condition they press
on their own finger with the other hand. In the slider condition a motor
produces the force and the participant sets its size with a slider.

Pressing directly they overshoot, and through the slider they are fairly
accurate. In the twenty-five-participant data published in McNaughton's device
paper the direct condition ran 0.50 N high on average and the slider condition
0.30 N low, and the difference between the two conditions is what the
measurement is.

## What the slider condition is for {.k-head}

Why the slider condition is needed is not obvious at first, and misreading the
task usually starts from there, so it is worth slowing down here.

The error in the direct condition has more than one source. You have to remember
the target force, you have to scale the force you produce, and on top of that
your motor output has noise of its own. None of these is specific to prediction,
and each produces a deviation on its own. The slider condition carries the same
memory and scaling load, but because the force does not come from your own hand
the prediction-based part is not engaged. Taking the difference between the two
conditions cancels the shared effects and leaves the share that belongs to
prediction.

This logic was tested formally not long ago. Valè and colleagues built a
computational model of the task on data from close to five hundred participants,
separated the noise sources including memory noise, and showed that the
difference between the two conditions does isolate the predictive component. Two
more things came out of the same study. Attenuated sensations are more variable
trial to trial, because they carry the noise of the prediction as well. And
attenuation works by division rather than subtraction: a fixed amount is not
taken off the signal, the signal is scaled down by a factor.

What the attenuation locks onto has been tested too. Bays and colleagues showed
that the mechanism is tied not to the movement itself but to the event the
movement is expected to produce. Shifting the timing of the touch forward or
back reduces attenuation, and movements that stop above the finger or pass
beside it produce none at all. So the system is not saying "I am moving, turn
the sensation down" so much as "a touch of this kind is about to happen here,
now". Kilteni and Ehrsson showed a more basic condition on top of that: you have to
count the touching hand as your own. When ownership is shifted with the rubber
hand illusion, the attenuation shifts with it.

## The link to precision {.k-head}

In the active inference framework, attenuation means lowering the precision of
sensory evidence during movement. The argument for calling it necessary is that
in order to move, the prediction that you are moving has to override the sensory
evidence saying you have not moved yet.
If the weight of that evidence is not lowered, the movement does not start.

Brown and colleagues reproduced the force-matching finding from this framework.
When they removed attenuation from the model the overshoot in the task
disappeared and false inferences about agency appeared. So the same setting both
makes movement possible and determines what counts as yours, and it costs you in
both directions: lower it too little and the movement does not start, lower it
too much and you cannot tell yourself from the world. Let me flag one thing
here. This comes out of a model and depends on what that model assumes; it is
not something an experiment has shown directly.

## Where it sits clinically {.k-head}

One of the oldest findings here still says the most. In 2000 Blakemore and
colleagues compared patients with schizophrenia, patients with bipolar disorder
and depression, and healthy controls. What determined the loss of attenuation
was the symptom rather than the diagnosis: it was absent in those with auditory
hallucinations or passivity experiences, and present in those without them
regardless of diagnosis.

What followed widened this. Attenuation was shown to be significantly reduced in
schizophrenia; in the imaging study, the loss of attenuation in secondary
somatosensory cortex tracked the patient's hallucination severity at the time.
Teufel and colleagues worked with healthy participants instead: those higher in
delusional ideation were more accurate on the task, meaning they attenuated
less. That last one answers two objections at once, because neither medication nor
an active episode can explain it.

It would be a mistake to stop at schizophrenia. In functional movement
disorder attenuation is absent; patients do not feel the movement as under their
own control and do not produce the overshoot controls produce. In Parkinson's
disease attenuation is selectively impaired in the group reporting fatigue and
not in the group without it, and the impairment tracks subjective fatigue and
perceived effort rather than motor symptom severity. In chronic pain no group
difference in magnitude was found; what separated the groups was variance.

That the impairment turns up across such different clinical pictures already
makes this a measure tied to a symptom rather than to a diagnosis. It does not
tell you which diagnosis a patient carries, it says something about which
mechanism is disturbed, and mixing the two up promises more than the measure can
give.
I am not claiming it has a use in the clinic today; these are group-level
differences and they do not tell you what to do in front of one patient.

## What the instrument contributes {.k-head}

Because the measurement is the difference between two conditions, any instrument
error that is the same in both conditions drops out of the difference. The error
that does not drop out is the one that depends on loading direction, since the
two conditions do not load the sensor the same way. A ramp pressed by a motor
and a ramp pressed by a person are not the same thing.

When I built my own rig, the item that passed its acceptance criterion by the
narrowest margin was hysteresis, and that is not a coincidence, because
hysteresis falls into exactly the class of error that does not cancel in the
difference. The rig itself and the calibration records are on the [instrument
page](../tools/force-matching.qmd).

## Reading a finding {.k-head}

The first thing to look at in a published attenuation finding is how many
conditions the design had. A deviation coming out of a single-condition design
cannot be called attenuation, because what strips out memory and scaling is the
second condition itself.

Then come the repetition count and the time window. In data from a hundred and
thirty-eight participants McNaughton and colleagues showed three things. The
number of repetitions can be brought down from eight, the best window for
extracting the matched force falls between 2.5 and 3.0 seconds, and performance
does not drift over the course of the experiment. If the choice of window is not
reported there is no way to compare two studies.

Last, whether the analysis looked only at the mean. In chronic pain the groups
did not separate in magnitude but did separate in variance, and an analysis
looking at the mean would never see a difference of that kind. Given that Valè
and colleagues' model says variability may be signal belonging to the prediction
rather than noise, it is hard to call this a small detail any more.

I will update this page as I collect my own data, particularly wherever what I
have written here turns out to be wrong.
